\subsection{JSD Decay Analysis}
\label{sec:jsd_extended}

The token-level JSD between adjacent generations reveals two distinct decay regimes (Figure~\ref{fig:jsd_decay}).
For C4 web text, 0v1 JSD exceeds 1v2 by 6--56$\times$ across all 7 models with $\Kempirical{=}2$ (median cliff ratio ${\sim}$15$\times$), and subsequent pairs converge to a noise floor of ${\sim}$0.003--0.005.
Fitting $\jsd(k, k{+}1) \propto e^{-\lambda k}$ yields $\lambda \approx 2.2$--$3.5$ for C4 (mean ${\approx}\,2.9$), consistent with rapid mixing of $G_\delta$ toward its stationary distribution.
These decay rates represent qualitative characterizations from 5-point curves rather than precise estimates.
The empirical decay rate $\lambda$ is consistent within each domain but varies across domains: C4 yields $\lambda \approx 2.9$, Wikipedia $\lambda \approx 3.1$ (excluding OLMo, whose $\lambda = 6.3$ reflects a capacity-limited collapse: 0v1 $\jsd = 0.169$ with near-complete information loss at the first step, making the exponential fit unreliable), and arXiv $\lambda \approx 1.0$.
This cross-model consistency indicates that the contraction rate of $G_\delta$ is governed primarily by the structure of the input domain rather than the model architecture.
ArXiv text decays ${\sim}$3$\times$ slower than C4 ($\lambda \approx 1.0$ vs.\ $2.9$), with a correspondingly higher convergence floor (${\sim}$0.007--0.009 vs.\ ${\sim}$0.003--0.004).
Formulaic structural features (LaTeX formatting, citation patterns, section templates) degrade more slowly under autoregressive generation and supply persistent depth-distinguishing signal, explaining the elevated $\Kempirical{=}3$.
The retrain-chain exhibits a fundamentally different profile: $\lambda = 0.285$ with a cliff ratio of only 1.31$\times$ and no sharp drop between adjacent pairs.
This gradual, sustained divergence reflects cumulative model-adaptation artifacts rather than text-intrinsic information loss, further supporting the distinction between prompt-chain and retrain-chain $\Kempirical$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:boundary_extended}).

\subsection{Boundary Cases and Scale Effect}
\label{sec:boundary_extended}

Of 8 tested model configurations on C4, 7 yield $\Kempirical{=}2$; Mistral-7B is the sole sub-2 exception ($\Kempirical{=}1$; 1v2 $\auc = 0.594$, CI $[0.584, 0.603]$), validating $\theta{=}0.60$ as an effective discriminator (gap: $0.594$ vs.\ $0.611$--$0.696$).
Mistral's cross-domain profile reinforces the domain-governed interpretation: despite $\Kempirical{=}1$ on both C4 and Wikipedia, it yields $\Kempirical{=}3$ on arXiv (1v2 $\auc = 0.820$, 2v3 $= 0.628$), and this profile persists under cross-scorer validation (Pythia-1.4B scorer: C4 $\Kempirical{=}1$, arXiv $\Kempirical{=}3$ (2v3 $\auc = 0.608$, CI $[0.593, 0.622]$)), indicating that domain structural complexity can rescue even web-text one-wash generators (Table~\ref{tab:domain_kstar}).
Larger models produce more human-like text, reducing 0v1 JSD: 0.16--0.29 at $\leq$1.5B, 0.077--0.13 at 7--8B (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-7B, Mistral-7B).
This trend suggests that models at 13B+ may increasingly yield $\Kempirical{=}1$; this speculative prediction warrants future verification.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We measure the generational depth discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.
$\Kempirical \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ depends on source domain and model characteristics: general web text yields $\Kempirical{=}2$ across 7/8 configurations (5 families, 1B--8B; $p \leq 0.002$), with $\Kempirical{=}3$ for academic text, confirmed across five models and four architecture families.
Generator-independent features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer ($\rho > 0.90$), making $\Kempirical$ measurement practical across generators.
As downstream validation, $\Kempirical{=}2$ supports binary filtering as the optimal granularity for web text: graduated depth weighting cannot exploit information that does not exist beyond the discrimination boundary.
$\Kempirical$ provides a representation-dependent lower bound on discriminable depth; the gap between $\Kempirical$ and the theoretical limit $\Ktheory$ remains open and may narrow with richer feature representations.
Future work includes scaling to 13B+, additional structured domains, and retrain-chain $\Kstar$ characterization.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

This gap cuts across multiple communities: binary detectors~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}), membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.

Knowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.
For data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.
Model collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.
$\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{First empirical measurement of $\Kempirical$} across 8 model configurations (5 architecture families, 1B--8B), 3 source domains, and 4 decoding strategies at $\theta{=}0.60$ ($p \leq 0.002$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
  Both supervised OBD and zero-shot frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) show no statistically significant difference beyond $\Kempirical$ (McNemar $p > 0.05$, $N{=}500$; Section~\ref{sec:why_kstar}).
  \item \textbf{Domain ordering invariance}: the hierarchy arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\Kempirical{=}1$) is preserved across six models spanning four architecture families, two scales (1B--8B), and four decoding strategies, with domain structural complexity as the primary factor governing $\Kempirical$ (Section~\ref{sec:cross_domain}).
  \item \textbf{Generator-independent features}: 15 scorer-derived statistical features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer among continuation-mode generators ($\rho > 0.90$ feature ranking preservation), making $\Kempirical$ measurement practical without generator-specific training (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a downstream validation, $\Kempirical{=}2$ correctly predicts the strategy ordering for web-text filtering: binary curation minimizes degradation most effectively (MMLU $0.5941$ vs.\ base $0.6018$; Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We measure the generational depth discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.
$\Kempirical \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ depends on source domain and model characteristics: general web text yields $\Kempirical{=}2$ across 7/8 configurations (5 families, 1B--8B; $p \leq 0.002$), with $\Kempirical{=}3$ for academic text, confirmed across five models and four architecture families.
Generator-independent features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer ($\rho > 0.90$), making $\Kempirical$ measurement practical across generators.
As downstream validation, $\Kempirical{=}2$ supports binary filtering as the optimal granularity for web text: graduated depth weighting cannot exploit information that does not exist beyond the discrimination boundary.
$\Kempirical$ provides a representation-dependent lower bound on discriminable depth; the gap between $\Kempirical$ and the theoretical limit $\Ktheory$ remains open and may narrow with richer feature representations.
Future work includes scaling to 13B+, additional structured domains, and retrain-chain $\Kstar$ characterization.
